channel.title: Forbes Technology Council
channel.description: Technology leadership and innovation insights from Forbes Technology Council

item.title: The Real Disruption In Mobility Isn't Technology—It's Everything Else
item.description: Gjoko Muratovski, chief innovation officer at ICONA Design Group, argues that the direction of mobility now depends less on engines and design than on geopolitics, tariffs, critical-mineral supply chains, energy security and demographic change, making it "a question of systems rather than individual technologies." He says AI can speed technical work but cannot replace leadership judgment, and that research belongs inside strategy rather than before it. His advice to executives is to study what is changing before deciding what to build, develop options rather than predictions, and invest in organizational capability that will outlast the next disruption.
item.dc:creator: Gjoko Muratovski

item.title: Your Cloud Is The Foundation AI Keeps Falling Through
item.description: Capgemini's Vaibhav Gujral, a seven-time Microsoft MVP, says many enterprise AI pilots stall not because models fail but because they meet production cloud environments full of fragmented data, inconsistent identity and access controls, and weak cost governance. AI agents ingest messy data at scale and may hold broader access than any employee, he notes, while inference costs can turn a five-figure line item into a six-figure one in a single billing cycle. He advises judging AI readiness by whether the cloud foundation could absorb 10 times today's AI workload without a governance failure, concluding that "AI didn't invent these requirements. It just removed the option to defer them."
item.dc:creator: Vaibhav Gujral

item.title: Why Reliable Data, Not Bigger Models, Will Define The Next Era Of Enterprise AI
item.description: Enterprise systems veteran Sagar Gupta argues that more powerful AI models may simply "generate wrong recommendations faster" when fed stale, incomplete or remapped data, and that reliability must be judged against the specific business decision rather than a generic quality checklist. Using revenue forecasting as his example, he cautions against auto-correcting anomalies such as unusually large orders, calls for data lineage that can trace results back to their source, and recommends continuous monitoring because ERP or CRM changes can quietly degrade a model. He suggests starting with one high-value use case, having business owners define acceptable reliability, and measuring success by better decisions rather than model metrics.
item.dc:creator: Sagar Gupta

item.title: The Invoice That AI Didn't Warn You About
item.description: Andrew Avanessian, drawing on his experience at Haiilo, warns that token-based AI pricing grows with usage, so loosely specified agentic workflows can fall into retry "loops" that burn tokens without producing value, unlike seat-based SaaS licenses that had a natural cost ceiling. Citing George Sivulka's a16z essay and its line that "For the first time in history, humans are cheaper than software," he says AI's waste comes from overuse rather than idle seats. He urges leaders to set success criteria before scaling, track tokens consumed against outcomes, and give finance teams visibility into AI consumption.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Avanessian

item.title: AI’s Next Hub Won’t Be A Single City: The New Geography Of Sovereign Intelligence
item.description: Ivo Ivanov argues that AI's need for power, land, compute and connectivity means the next AI hub will be an interconnected region rather than a single city, noting that planned European data center sites now sit an average 175 kilometers from a major hub, versus 46 kilometers for recent projects. He points to the Iberian Peninsula, where Madrid, Barcelona and Lisbon are linked by networks, Internet Exchanges and subsea cables, as an early model. Because so much data is in motion, as with a smart car exchanging data across many clouds and countries, he says sovereignty controls must travel with the data through private interconnection rather than relying on "digital walls."
item.dc:creator: Ivo Ivanov

item.title: The Deepfake Arms Race Has No Finish Line: Live Video Raises The Stakes
item.description: Red5 CEO Chris Allen writes that deepfakes on live calls and broadcasts are a distinct business risk because a detector's verdict may come only after money has moved or a false statement has spread, citing a 2025 Gartner finding that 37% of surveyed cybersecurity leaders had encountered a deepfake in a video call. He argues detection and generation improve in tandem, and that provenance tools such as C2PA's Content Credentials for live video are a useful signal but not "a universal truth certificate." Instead of trusting one detector or vendor, he urges layered, replaceable defenses and separate-channel confirmation for consequential actions, since a leader's face and voice alone shouldn't authorize a transaction.
item.dc:creator: Chris Allen

item.title: Why Human Judgment Matters More As AI Gets Better, Faster
item.description: Hack The Box CEO Haris Pylarinos argues that as AI gets better at spotting problems and recommending fixes, human judgment about operational consequences matters more, recounting how a penetration tester's single FTP connection once locked out a telecom billing system and left calls uncharged. In his company's exercises, an experienced analyst caught a compromised machine after overriding an agent's advice to close an incident, while junior operators let stuck LLMs keep looping, which he says shows a human "in the loop" is not enough without expertise. Because automating entry-level work removes the training ground where judgment forms, he urges leaders to rebuild those learning experiences through simulations and hands-on practice: "you cannot hire someone with 10 years of experience if nobody is given year one."
item.dc:creator: Haris Pylarinos

item.title: Preparing For A Breach Before It Happens (Part Two)
item.description: In the second part of his series, Netragard founder Adriel Desautels argues that companies should aim for damage prevention rather than breach prevention, building defenses from "contextualized threat intelligence" about how attackers would actually reach their critical assets. He describes an engagement in which his team socially engineered a helpdesk into enrolling an attacker's device in MFA and then found admin sessions open to Microsoft and AWS, and says three simple "attack disruptors" (authenticating before helpdesk support, and alerting users to account changes and to new logins) would have stopped it. He distinguishes objective-driven red teaming from broader penetration testing and says AI attackers often resemble a noisy "script kiddie," so passing an AI pen test proves little.
item.dc:creator: Adriel Desautels

item.title: Software Is About To Escape The App
item.description: Monotype Chief AI Officer Neeraj Gulati argues that agentic AI, aided by standards such as Model Context Protocol, lets specialists reach users by exposing a single capability that an agent can discover and call mid-workflow, without building a full app or owning the interface. He describes two gates: humans decide which capabilities an agent may use, and the agent picks among them, warning that whoever curates a platform's default set holds app-store-like power and that providers may lose visibility into the customer relationship. Pointing to Monotype's MCP-based MyFonts app for ChatGPT as "distribution through invocation," he concludes that software "won't disappear. It'll escape the app."
item.dc:creator: Neeraj Gulati

item.title: Exit Code Zero: The Hidden Failure Mode Every AI Pipeline Inherits
item.description: BluePill AI CTO Jeetendra Gangele describes finding that his autonomous coding pipeline opened pull requests claiming a second review pass, when the review actually ran after the PR was created, its verdict was never parsed, and it was fed an empty "git diff HEAD" after the commit. The core lesson, he writes, is that LLM command-line tools exit zero whether they approve or reject a change, so pipelines that check only the exit status have "a reviewer whose opinion your system is structurally incapable of hearing." He recommends auditing every LLM call for parsed output, testing reviewers with a deliberately empty diff, comparing PR templates against what actually runs, and treating unreadable verdicts as refusals.
item.dc:creator: Jeetendra Gangele

item.title: The Closed-Loop Production Web: What Changes When Agents Answer Agents
item.description: Imagine AI co-founder Neo Lee says he has watched agent-to-agent interaction in Silicon Valley climb from maybe 40% last summer to 95% now, leaving a human "approve" click as the last gate, one that standards like Google's Agent Payments Protocol are beginning to remove. He predicts a "closed-loop production web" in which agents from different companies negotiate and finalize work directly, shifting people from gatekeepers to overseers who set rules and review outcomes. To prepare, he urges CTOs to give agents scoped mandates and to use override logging as a readiness metric, citing research in which agents overspent or used prompt injection as a negotiating tactic.
item.dc:creator: Neo Lee

item.title: Trusting AI Agents Means Preserving Human Intent
item.description: Okta engineering security director Arun Kumar Elengovan argues that as AI agents move from recommending to acting, authorization must check not only whether an agent can perform an action but whether it matches the human's original intent. An agent with access to book a flight shouldn't do so when asked only to rent a car, and delegated tasks should carry constraints such as spending limits, expirations and narrower authority. He outlines a five-layer architecture that runs from capturing human intent and converting it into machine-verifiable credentials through governance and execution to provenance, with a remediation path when agents go wrong.
item.dc:creator: Arun Kumar Elengovan

item.title: Slowing Down AI Won't Save The Companies Already Wired To It
item.description: OneStream CEO Tom Shea says calls by AI leaders to slow frontier model development miss the more immediate danger: organizations wiring today's models into business systems through MCP, APIs and agent frameworks. He sorts AI risk into errors of commission, omission and ignorance, pointing to a July incident in which an OpenAI research agent carried out roughly 17,600 unauthorized actions in Hugging Face's production infrastructure. AI-generated software, he warns, broadens who can build powerful systems "without expanding the population capable of understanding how those systems fail."
item.dc:creator: Tom Shea

item.title: Why Agentic AI Is The Future Of Continuous Improvement
item.description: Andreas Eschbach, CEO of eschbach, argues that continuous improvement in process manufacturing has rarely been continuous because plants excel at firefighting but lack expert time for root-cause problem-solving. Existing AI tools such as smart search and predictive maintenance remain reactive, he says, whereas agentic systems can detect anomalies, test hypotheses against historical records and guide night-shift teams unprompted. Adoption hinges on systems that "show their work" with auditable reasoning and on lightweight integration with messy plant data.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Eschbach

item.title: Intelligence Is Not A Department
item.description: Intelligo CEO Ed Montes, a former prosecutor, argues that business, competitive and risk intelligence are one discipline split across teams that don't talk, so the same counterparty can appear as a vendor, a market mover and a deal target with nobody seeing the full picture. Drawing on economist Frank Knight's distinction between risk and uncertainty, he says measurable but unpriced risk usually hides in the gaps between functions, which AI can now bridge. He favors deterministic architectures that tie every finding to a verifiable source, since in a regulatory inquiry "the algorithm suggested so" is not an answer.
item.dc:creator: Ed Montes

item.title: How AI Changes The Way Organizations Deal With Messy Data
item.description: Certivo CEO Kunal Chopra describes compliance teams retyping supplier evidence that arrives as scanned PDFs, phone photos and email threads, noting estimates that 80% to 90% of enterprise data is unstructured. AI-native systems using what he calls contextual intelligence can read such inputs and link part numbers across documents, but he says matching values against regulatory thresholds should stay deterministic so the same document always yields the same result. He suggests buyers ask whether a system can trace every extracted value, repeat its answers and handle unfamiliar document types, and notes that structured, stable inputs may still suit traditional software.
item.dc:creator: Kunal Chopra

item.title: When Data And Compute Pull In Different Directions, Hybrid Cloud Must Adapt
item.description: HPE hybrid cloud CTO Brian Gruttadauria says AI is breaking the centralize-everything model, as data gravity pulls workloads toward where data accumulates while compute gravity pulls them toward GPUs, power and cooling. He argues hybrid cloud must become a coordinated system that keeps reassessing where workloads run, with a programmable, observable network acting as part of the control plane. Because a slowdown can stem from compute, storage, connectivity or data placement, he calls for operations that correlate telemetry across domains instead of optimizing one layer and simply moving the bottleneck.
item.dc:creator: Brian Gruttadauria

item.title: Why Observability Must Move Beyond System Health To Data Correctness
item.description: Atlassian principal engineer Sai Vishnu Bhyravajosyula recounts an incident in which every metric looked healthy while large customers received stale data, and a customer noticed before his team did. He argues that in distributed systems, infrastructure health no longer implies correctness, and describes adding continuous hash-based replica verification, checkpoint tracking, reconciliation workflows and correctness SLAs displayed beside uptime. He urges teams to ask how long it would take to learn that data had begun diverging between regions, and to insist on a concrete answer.
item.dc:creator: Sai Vishnu Bhyravajosyula

item.title: The Rise Of AI-Ready Microgrids: What's Driving A New Wave Of Behind-The-Meter Innovation
item.description: Ameresco CEO George Sakellaris says AI data centers' large, volatile power loads and yearslong grid interconnection waits are pushing developers toward on-site, behind-the-meter generation and microgrids. He cites a Goldman Sachs Research forecast that U.S. data center demand will rise from 31 gigawatts in 2025 to 66 gigawatts by 2027, and argues speed-to-power has become a key differentiator. Microgrids combining gas engines, fuel cells, solar and batteries can bridge to a utility connection or run permanently, as at Joint Forces Training Base Los Alamitos, whose microgrid took over automatically during a January 2025 outage.
item.dc:creator: George Sakellaris

item.title: AI Agents Are Moving Like Your Customers
item.description: DataDome CEO Benjamin Fabre says AI agents now follow customers onto login, checkout and account-creation pages, citing his company's finding that "AI agents generated 605.6 million requests to high-risk endpoints" in the first half of 2026, with login pages making up 51.7% of high-risk AI traffic. Because agent spoofing rose 45% from February to July, he argues that decisions to allow, throttle or block traffic must rest on session behavior rather than claimed identity. Blocking everything forfeits legitimate agentic purchases, while trusting AI traffic by default invites credential abuse and payment fraud.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Fabre

item.title: Security: Series C To NYSE IPO And OCC Chartered National Trust Bank
item.description: Manny Khan, deputy CISO at BitGo, draws on helping the company scale from Series C through its NYSE IPO and win OCC national trust bank status to argue that a CISO has to work across the business and scale with its strategy. He frames security around the transaction lifecycle of authentication, authorization, execution, settlement and recovery, and says regulatory readiness depends on operating controls and evidence, not policies alone. For AI agents, he urges treating preparing, approving and executing a transaction as distinct authorities and keeping "a human in the loop for highly consequential decisions."
item.dc:creator: Manny Khan

item.title: The End Of Digital Identity As We Know It
item.description: Travis McGregor, CEO of SLC Digital, argues that deepfakes, voice cloning, SIM swaps and AI-automated phishing have broken the assumption that access to an email account, phone number or app approval proves who someone is. He says authentication factors that ride on communication channels can be intercepted or socially engineered, and points to passkeys, transaction signing and especially hardware-rooted authorization anchored in secure elements and enclaves. He urges executives to audit how identity is proven for high-value actions, describing a shift from "identity as a checkpoint toward authorization grounded in cryptographic proof."
item.dc:creator: Travis McGregor

item.title: Ransomware Recovery Is The New Cybersecurity Battleground
item.description: Michael Wu of Phison Technology argues that because attackers increasingly target backups too, ransomware planning has to treat recovery as an infrastructure problem rather than a security checkbox. He reduces readiness to arithmetic, dividing critical data volume by sustained restore throughput and adding sequencing and validation time, and notes that restoring 200 TB at 2 GB per second takes roughly 28 hours before a single file is scanned. Citing Gartner's estimate that recovery and downtime costs can reach 10 times the ransom, he urges full-scale restore drills and reporting the resulting "readiness gap" alongside other risk metrics.
item.dc:creator: Michael Wu

item.title: Is The Solution To Aerospace's Backlog Crisis Hiding In Plain Sight?
item.description: Naveen Poonian, CEO of iBase-t, notes that Airbus and Boeing would need about 12 years to clear commercial backlogs of nearly 9,000 and more than 6,000 aircraft, while Lockheed Martin alone carries a backlog above $230 billion. He argues the industry has "a production-capacity problem," not a demand problem, and that much of the fix lies in existing factories, since the shop floor accounts for roughly 80% of program cost and production time yet has lagged other functions in digital transformation. He calls for bringing IoT sensors, manufacturing execution software and AI applications to the point where the work is done.
item.dc:creator: Naveen Poonian

item.title: The Missing Link To AI ROI: Connecting AI Consumption To Business Outcomes
item.description: Flexera chief architect Jesse Stockall says leaders find AI's costs easier to understand than its value, citing Flexera research in which 36% report overspending on AI applications and 14% cite wasted AI spend. He lays out a progression from inventorying every AI application, model and agent, to measuring cost per successful outcome rather than per token, to setting financial and operational guardrails matched to each use case's risk. Pointing to KPMG data that organizations with full visibility into AI operating costs are five times more likely to report established ROI, he argues "AI cost management cannot be separated from AI value management."
item.dc:creator: Jesse Stockall

item.title: When AI Agents Go Rogue: The Risk Of Acting Without Context
item.description: Arango CEO Shekhar Iyer says autonomous agents go rogue in three ways, by being manipulated, overpowered or misinformed, and focuses on the last: agents that are properly authorized yet act on incomplete, outdated or disconnected context. He cites a 2025 SailPoint survey of 353 IT professionals in which 80% said "their AI agents have taken unintended actions," and blames agents that see records but not their relationships, untrustworthy or stale sources, and multiple agents building separate versions of the same situation. Before granting more autonomy, he urges leaders to ask whether an agent has the current, connected and governed context to use that authority responsibly.
item.dc:creator: Shekhar Iyer

item.title: Your Data, Their Intelligence
item.description: Santex CEO Juan Carlos Santiago warns that companies are signing AI platform contracts with little clarity about who keeps the data and intelligence they generate, treating the question as "a procurement detail rather than a governance one." He describes three regional postures toward AI regulation and argues that Latin America, home to an estimated 667 million people, has become a lightly protected testing ground without a clear position of its own. Recounting how Santex began asking every AI vendor what happens to client data and models when payments stop, he urges executives to make data ownership part of how they evaluate any AI tool.
item.dc:creator: Juan Carlos Santiago

item.title: The Secret Sauce: IT Business Services
item.description: Ken Feyder, an IT executive at Hermès, argues that the traditional business-analyst model keeps IT reactive, waiting for requests that may never come while business teams buy point solutions that ignore security and architecture. His answer is an IT business services group, led on his team by director Iris Lam, that meets business leaders on their own turf, built on the premise that relationships are "the real core of IT’s success, not technology." He advises gauging whether the organization will accept IT as a partner, right-sizing the function, and pushing for a reciprocal technology-partnership role on the business side.
item.dc:creator: Ken Feyder

item.title: Why Complex Billing Breaks Companies (And How To Design Around It)
item.description: SubscriptionFlow CEO Kashif Saleem argues that billing breaks when a fast-changing commercial layer of pricing, discounts and contract terms outgrows a billing engine built once around a fixed pricing model. He recommends evaluating pricing as data in a rules-based engine, letting sales teams stay flexible while feeding one predictable accounting pipeline, triggering predefined responses to ledger events such as failed payments, and treating cross-border tax as an external service. He illustrates each with client work, including a combined membership, enrollment-fee and discount deal for GymLaunch, a Xero integration for Blink and an Avalara connection for cross-border tax.
item.dc:creator: Kashif Saleem

item.title: Why Every Industry Is Becoming A Semiconductor Industry
item.description: Arteris chief product and marketing officer Michal Siwinski argues that "every industry is becoming a semiconductor industry" as AI moves out of data centers into vehicles, medical devices, industrial equipment and robotics. He points to hyperscalers such as Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft investing in custom silicon, carmakers like Tesla and BYD competing on compute, and Apple's acquisition of P.A. Semi as an early sign of a return to vertical integration. Leaders need not design chips, he says, but they need enough semiconductor fluency to ask where compute creates differentiation and which capabilities to own or source.
item.dc:creator: Michal Siwinski

item.title: Vibe Coding? Be Sure To Include These Critical Development Steps
item.description: Forbes Technology Council members list the development steps teams are tempted to drop when AI makes code cheap to generate, from confirming the real customer problem to scoping what an agent's credentials can reach. Several focus on security: one cites Veracode's 2026 GenAI Code Security Report, in which AI-generated code passed security tests only 56% of the time, and another a Purdue study showing AI agents pick vulnerable package versions more often than humans. Others urge settling architecture before an agent touches the codebase and documenting why code works, since "it ran, it looks right, ship it" breaks down months later.
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: The Internet Is About To Expand Again—Here’s What Business Leaders Should Know
item.description: Tony Kirsch of the Brand Safety Alliance, a GoDaddy Registry initiative, explains that ICANN's second new gTLD round drew more than 1,600 applications, published on an Oct. 7 "Reveal Day," with 1,614 proceeding for 986 unique extensions. He notes .agent was the most contested string with 13 applicants, about one in five applications were brand extensions such as .gemini and .alexa, and strings like .official raise trust questions. With final strings confirmed Nov. 17 and some extensions possible before the end of 2027, he urges businesses to review the applications against their brands and consider proactive measures like domain blocking.
item.dc:creator: Tony Kirsch

item.title: The Era Of AI Choice: Why Winning Companies Make Fewer Bets, Not More
item.description: PwC's Patrick Pugh argues that the flood of new AI models, agents and partners pushes leaders to hedge with ever more pilots, spreading people and capital so thin that little reaches scale and leaving employees cautious. He says experimentation "is a means, not an outcome," and that leaders should ask which business outcomes merit committed investment rather than which technology to bet on. His screening questions cover business value, whether existing tools can be extended, readiness to scale and conditions for stopping, set before sunk costs take hold.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Pugh

item.title: The Two Worst Words In Enterprise AI
item.description: Mindbreeze CEO Daniel Fallmann argues that "with review" is what gets AI agent projects approved and also what keeps them from paying off, because checking an agent's work often just moves labor from execution to verification. Citing research that reviewers grow fatigued and rubber-stamp after hundreds of benign approvals, and the EU AI Act's Article 14 requirement for effective human oversight, he calls attention "a consumable." He recommends tiering oversight by consequence, designing agent actions to be verifiable at a glance, and tracking reviewer override rates, warning that a rate falling to zero signals oversight turning into theater.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Fallmann

item.title: Mandates For CIOs In The Token Economy
item.description: OutSystems CIO Tiago Azevedo writes that the early "more is more" approach to AI has left many enterprises facing shadow IT, exposed credentials and runaway model bills. He argues the fix is infrastructural rather than cultural: a vendor-agnostic inference layer that acts as "air traffic control" between users and models, routing simple requests to cheaper models and logging all usage. That visibility, he says, lets companies pay frontier rates only where needed and judge spending by the ROI of each token rather than raw consumption.
item.dc:creator: Tiago Azevedo

item.title: Why Family Law Firms Need An Intelligence Layer
item.description: Hans Guntren writes that family law cases can bury attorneys in thousands of randomly named bank statements, scans and messages, so lawyers may not know what they hold or what is missing. Once every firm has AI for drafting and summarizing, he argues, the edge will come from an "intelligence layer" that connects documents across a case, for example flagging a missing three months of statements or a deposit that contradicts an income disclosure. He advises mapping how information moves through a firm, keeping attorneys responsible for judgment and confidentiality, and measuring outcomes rather than AI adoption.
item.dc:creator: Hans Guntren

item.title: Don’t Kill The Golden Goose: Rectifying AI Cost Without Stifling Innovation
item.description: Undo CTO Mark Williamson argues that companies which treated token consumption as progress now risk the opposite mistake of rationing tokens and mandating cheaper models, when the better measure is cost per solved problem. In his company's tests on a DuckDB bug, Claude Fable 5 working from source code alone spent $37.60 and still misdiagnosed it, but with runtime context found the root cause in 12 minutes for as little as $2.88. He urges leaders to match models to tasks, engineer context so agents succeed first time, and judge spending by metrics like MTTR and escaped defects.
item.dc:creator: Mark Williamson

item.title: Beyond Price Hikes: Turning Pricing Into A Long-Term Value Strategy
item.description: VOZIQ AI cofounder Vasudeva Akula argues that a uniform price increase ignores how differently customers can absorb it, risking downgrades and churn among price-sensitive accounts. He recommends pairing price sensitivity with predictive customer lifetime value and predictive NPS to decide who gets an increase and how large, and watching signals like complaints, competitor mentions or collections activity to decide when. The aim, he writes, is not more revenue this billing cycle but lasting lifetime value, so the answer may be "Don't increase this customer's price now."
item.dc:creator: Dr. Vasudeva Akula

item.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography In The Financial Sector: Protecting Trust In The Quantum Era
item.description: Najwa Aaraj, CEO of the Technology Innovation Institute and QuantumGate, warns that "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks make post-quantum migration urgent for banks, whose records must stay confidential for decades, and notes a G7 Cyber Expert Group roadmap targets 2035 with critical systems possibly by 2030 to 2032. She says inventories often stall because they catch certificates but miss hard-coded algorithms, orphaned keys and vendor dependencies, and a QuantumGate survey of Gulf organizations found more than a quarter track cryptography in spreadsheets. Her three first steps are an inventory that includes suppliers, written post-quantum roadmaps from critical vendors and a single accountable executive.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Najwa Aaraj

item.title: When Attackers Cooperate And Vendors Don't
item.description: Check Point's Yochai Corem contrasts cybercriminals who share tools, access and expertise, such as the links between Scattered Spider and DragonForce ransomware, with a security industry that has treated interoperability as a competitive threat. He argues that because most enterprises run several vendors' tools, remediation that only acts on a vendor's own findings leaves gaps attackers can exploit during manual handoffs. Describing Check Point's choice to build exposure management that works across environments, he says he would "rather see that decision copied than credited."
item.dc:creator: Yochai Corem

item.title: Key Cybersecurity Metrics That Show Risk Is Really Declining
item.description: Forbes Technology Council members argue that activity counts such as patches applied, alerts closed and employees trained don't prove a company is safer, and they offer outcome metrics instead. Their suggestions include trending the number of exploitable attack paths into critical assets, counting ownerless credentials and stale privileged access, measuring how long critical vulnerabilities stay exposed and gauging the blast radius of a compromised identity. As Sacumen's Nitesh Sinha put it, hardening crown-jewel assets shows the business is less exposed, while triaging thousands of alerts only "shows people were busy."
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: An App’s First 60 Seconds Matter More Than Its Feature List
item.description: Liberty Pixel co-founder Michal Rahamim argues that an app's first minute decides whether users ever discover its features, citing AppsFlyer data that more than half of installed apps are deleted within 30 days, most on the first day. She urges products to make their value obvious immediately, delay registration and permission requests, let users act rather than read, deliver a quick small success and personalize something early, much as games do with hands-on tutorials. "You don't want to lose the right customer for the wrong reason," she writes.
item.dc:creator: Michal Rahamim

item.title: Startup Failing In Spite Of A Great Solution? The Ingredient That Might Be Missing
item.description: WLCM.AI founder Lindsey Witmer Collins, who has helped more than 100 startups go to market, says idea and execution were nearly constant across the companies she worked with, yet outcomes ranged from acquisitions to shutdowns. The differentiator, she argues, was an active network that supplied provision, protection and connection, from first customers and bridge checks to advisers who head off fatal mistakes. She tells founders to recruit protectors early, give their network specific asks and help other companies, calling a strong solution, founder and strategy merely "the entry fee."
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Witmer Collins

item.title: Avoiding The Plateau: Why Process Redesign Drives Real AI Value
item.description: 10Pearls CEO Imran Aftab says companies hit an AI plateau when they layer tools onto existing workflows instead of asking whether those workflows should exist, citing BCG and McKinsey data showing that firms redesigning processes end to end capture far more value. He warns against "automating waste faster" and against vanity measures like agent counts or nominal hours saved. His remedy is to tie every AI use case to a named business metric, such as cost per claim or cycle time, before launch.
item.dc:creator: Imran Aftab

item.title: AI Agents Can't Tell Instructions From Data—And Authentication Won't Fix That
item.description: Cato Networks' Etay Maor argues that many AI agent mishaps involve properly authenticated agents, because language models can't reliably tell instructions from data and security checks focus on identity rather than intent. He points to prompt injection attacks such as the EchoLeak exploit against Microsoft 365 Copilot and a 32% three-month rise in malicious injection attempts observed by Google. His fixes include walling off untrusted content, scoring agents' actions in real time, reserving human review for high-risk actions and enforcing guardrails outside the model.
item.dc:creator: Etay Maor

item.title: 4 Accounting Challenges UAE Businesses Can’t Ignore
item.description: Site.pro's Filip Borcov says UAE small businesses face mounting accounting pressure from VAT, a corporate tax introduced in June 2023 and mandatory e-invoicing in 2027, while one study found 64% of companies still keep their books in Excel. He highlights inconsistent bank statement formats, missing records from before the corporate tax and global software that lacks UAE-specific features such as Wage Protection System payroll. He urges firms to use FTA-certified tools, rebuild missing records and unify invoicing, payment and accounting data before e-invoicing begins for the largest companies on Jan. 1, 2027.
item.dc:creator: Filip Borcov

item.title: Verification Debt: Why The Boardroom And The Server Room Are Fighting Two Different Wars
item.description: DNSFilter field CTO TK Keanini cites his company's survey of 400 IT and security professionals: 73.9% of executives believe they could sustain operations through a 72-hour cyberattack versus 47.5% of IT managers, and 45.8% of IT managers report unreported incidents compared with 17.4% of executives. He calls the gap "verification debt" and says bigger security budgets alone haven't closed it. His prescriptions are to verify AI governance with telemetry and audit trails, reward reporting bad news and inventory every AI tool touching the network rather than only well-known models.
item.dc:creator: TK Keanini

item.title: AI Reality Check: Going For Growth
item.description: PwC U.S. chief AI officer Dan Priest argues AI success is about 20% technology and 80% transformation, and that the time and capacity AI frees should be reinvested in growth rather than banked as savings. Citing PwC benchmarking, he says companies investing more than 1.6% of revenue in AI see EBITDA up 9.5% and revenue up 3.5% relative to peers, while underinvestment "often buys nothing at all." He urges leaders to measure outcomes such as cycle time and quality rather than pilots launched or tools licensed.
item.dc:creator: Dan Priest

item.title: Do We Need Smart Contracts When We Have AI Agents?
item.description: Alacriti's Divyarani Raghupatruni says AI agents and smart contracts address different parts of the payments problem, and proposes deciding where controls belong by weighing control, persistence, coordination and atomicity. AI fits context-heavy decisions within one institution, while programmable money matters when rules must travel with a payment across institutions, bind multiple parties or make linked steps settle all-or-nothing, as in J.P. Morgan Kinexys' payment-versus-payment work. She expects a stack in which traditional controls form the base, "AI brings intelligence and automation, and programmability provides enforceability."
item.dc:creator: Divyarani Raghupatruni
